issues.legal_issue: In an urgent land acquisition, the required newspaper publication and local notice need not be completed before the declaration of public purpose is published, provided the Gazette notification precedes the Gazette declaration by at least one day and the required publication steps are completed.
material_facts: Land was acquired to rehabilitate families displaced by airport land acquisition.
The Government invoked urgency to dispense with the hearing and to direct possession to be taken.
The Gazette recorded publication of the acquisition notification on December 23, 1986, and of the declaration on December 24, 1986.
Publication in newspapers and notice of the notification's substance in the locality occurred later.
Possession was taken on January 29, 1987, and the Collector made the awards on December 23, 1987.
issues.conclusion: The newspaper and local-notice steps were mandatory overall, but they did not have to be completed before publication of the declaration or the exercise of urgency powers. A gap of at least one day between Gazette publication of the notification and declaration was sufficient.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1), 5-A, 6(1) and (3), and 17(1), (2) and (4) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Gazette publication of the notification and declaration is required, and the declaration makes the public purpose conclusive. The three Section 4(1) publication steps are mandatory, but their sequence must be read in light of the urgent-possession purpose of Section 17: the newspaper and local-notice steps need not precede the declaration. State of Haryana v. Raghubir Dayal treated the Section 4(1) steps as mandatory and the later Section 6(2) publication steps as directory; Krishi Utpadan Samiti v. Makrand Singh addressed the limitation purpose of “hereinafter”; State of U.P. v. Radhey Shyam Nigam required the declaration to follow the notification but did not decide the required time gap. The Court applied the interpretive approach in State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya, under which statutory language is read in context, purpose and consequences.

rule.if: urgent_land_acquisition and government_dispensed_with_hearing and gazette_notification_preceded_gazette_declaration_by_at_least_one_day and required_publication_steps_were_completed

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition: The proceeding concerned acquisition of land for a public purpose under an asserted need for urgency.
predicates.government_dispensed_with_hearing: The Government dispensed with the affected owners' opportunity to object and directed urgent possession.
predicates.gazette_notification_preceded_gazette_de: The Gazette publication of the acquisition notification occurred at least one day before Gazette publication of the declaration.
predicates.required_publication_steps_were_complete: The notification was published in the required newspapers and its substance was publicly noticed at convenient places in the locality.
predicates.later_newspaper_and_local_notice_do_not_: The acquisition remains valid even though newspaper publication and local notice followed the declaration.

issues.definition: When an urgent acquisition has the required Gazette sequence and the required publication steps are completed, later newspaper publication and local notice do not invalidate it.

issues.legal_issue: The Gazette dates stated for publication, rather than the dates on which the Gazette was physically printed, determine the sequence of the notification and declaration.
material_facts: The Gazette recorded the notification and declaration as published on December 23 and December 24, 1986, respectively.
The physical Gazettes were printed on January 28 and January 29, 1987, respectively.
The parties disputed which dates controlled whether the declaration followed the notification.
issues.conclusion: The dates of publication stated in the Gazette were conclusive; the later dates of physical printing did not control.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 require publication of the notification and declaration. Under Section 17(4), the declaration must be published after the notification. The Court held that the Gazette publication dates, rather than actual printing dates, establish that sequence. It considered State of U.P. v. Radhey Shyam Nigam, which held that “after” means subsequent to publication but did not decide the required gap, and State of Haryana v. Raghubir Dayal on the publication requirements.

predicates.land_acquisition_publication_dispute: The proceeding concerns the order or timing of publications in a land acquisition.
predicates.gazette_records_publication_dates: The Gazette states dates on which the notification and declaration were published.
predicates.physical_printing_occurred_later: The Gazette was physically printed after the publication dates it records.
predicates.gazette_recorded_dates_control_publicati: The dates stated in the Gazette determine whether the notification preceded the declaration.

issues.definition: In a land-acquisition publication dispute, when the Gazette records publication dates but is printed later, the recorded dates determine the sequence.

issues.legal_issue: When an appellate court reverses an order quashing a declaration, the original declaration is restored, and a later republication is unnecessary and has no independent effect.
material_facts: A single judge quashed the declaration published on December 24, 1986.
The appellate court reversed that decision and dismissed the challenge to the acquisition.
A further declaration was published on May 19, 1995, after the single judge's ruling.
The land had already been taken into possession and the original award had been made.
issues.conclusion: The appellate reversal restored the original declaration; the later declaration was superfluous and had no effect on the restored declaration.
issues.legal_principle: Publication of a declaration under Section 6(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 is mandatory and gives conclusiveness to the public purpose under Section 6(3). An appeal is a continuation of the original proceedings, so reversal of the order quashing a declaration restores the declaration. Khadim Hussain v. State of U.P. concerned the form and authorization of a declaration, while the Court noted that the question of publication after making the declaration was not decided there.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and original_declaration_was_quashed_at_first_instance and appellate_court_reversed_quashing_order and later_declaration_was_published

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a declaration made in a land acquisition.
predicates.original_declaration_was_quashed_at_firs: A first-instance court set aside the original declaration.
predicates.appellate_court_reversed_quashing_order: An appellate court reversed the order setting aside the declaration.
predicates.later_declaration_was_published: The acquiring authority published another declaration after the first-instance ruling.
predicates.original_declaration_is_restored_and_lat: The original declaration has effect again, and the later declaration adds no legal effect.

issues.definition: If an appellate court reverses the quashing of an original acquisition declaration, that declaration is restored and a later declaration is superfluous.

issues.legal_issue: After possession has been taken and the land has vested absolutely in the State, the Government cannot withdraw from the acquisition under the statutory withdrawal power.
material_facts: Possession of the acquired land was taken on January 29, 1987.
The land thereby vested absolutely in the State free from encumbrances.
The awards had been made, and the Court considered whether the Government retained a power to withdraw after vesting.
issues.conclusion: Once possession had been taken and the land had vested absolutely, the Government could no longer withdraw from the acquisition under the statutory withdrawal power.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 16 and 17 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 provide for vesting upon possession in the circumstances addressed by those provisions; after vesting free from encumbrances, Section 48(1) does not permit withdrawal. The Court distinguished Lt. Governor of Himachal Pradesh v. Sri Avinash Sharma, which held that after vesting the Government could not use Section 21 of the General Clauses Act to withdraw the declaration.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a compulsory acquisition of land.
predicates.possession_was_taken_under_acquisition: The acquiring authority took possession of the land under the acquisition process.
predicates.land_vested_absolutely_in_state: The land vested in the State free from encumbrances.
predicates.government_cannot_withdraw_from_acquisit: The Government no longer has power to withdraw from the acquisition.

issues.definition: When possession has been taken in an acquisition and the land has vested absolutely in the State, the Government cannot withdraw from that acquisition.
